title: Amrit when you're ready
hookLine: five stood up in 1699, each by his own choice; amrit waits for your yes
carry: amrit waits for your own yes
tomorrow: Simran gets her first job. what makes money clean?

cards: Every family dinner has one relative who asks the question everyone else was too polite to ask. In Simran's family it's Chacha Ji, her dad's younger brother, between the dal and the rice: so, Simran, when's your amrit?
Jasleen took it, no? The table goes quiet. Harjit stares at his plate.
Bebe Jaswant puts down her spoon.

teach.h: VAISAKHI 1699: WHO WILL GIVE HIS HEAD?
teach.b: Bebe's answer is short. Some take it young. Some take it with gray hair.
I took it after you were born, she tells Chacha Ji, and nobody hurried me. Then she tells the story every Sikh child knows. Vaisakhi, 1699, at Anandpur.
A great crowd has gathered. Guru Gobind Singh comes out with a sword and asks: who will give his head? Silence.
Then one man stands. The Guru asks again, and again, until five have stood. Each one rose on his own; nobody was pulled from his seat.

teach.h: FIVE STOOD UP, EACH ON HIS OWN.
teach.b: Those five became the Panj Pyare, the five beloved, the first to receive amrit, and to this day five Sikhs give it.
That's the teaching under the dinner question: amrit is a lifelong commitment, so it has to be your own yes.
The Sikh code sets no age; it asks that a person be willing and old enough to understand.
Look back over the week: the head already on the palm, the daily banis and five Ks, the five who give, a new beginning, and not yet is fine.

teach.h: THE PACE BELONGS TO THE PERSON.
teach.b: They all say one thing to Chacha Ji: the pace belongs to the person.
Simran says it herself, smiling: I'm thinking about it. When I'm ready, you'll be the first to know. Chacha Ji laughs and asks for more rice.

how: Sikh families and gurdwaras encourage amrit, and the step itself is left to the person, taken when they are ready.

o: letting each person come to amrit at their own speed
the speed of the kirtan sung at the ceremony
everyone taking amrit together on one set day

games.q: a week of lines — tap the pairs.
p: the head already on the palm
stumbles come with a way back
no check at the gurdwara door

s: the Sikh code sets an age by which amrit must be taken
it sets no age; it asks that a person be willing and old enough to understand.
pushing someone toward amrit helps them get ready faster
readiness is the head already on the palm; nobody pushes it there.
in 1699, the Guru picked five men out of the crowd and brought them forward
he asked, and each of the five stood up on his own; amrit still waits for a person's own yes.

games.q: at gurdwara camp, a younger kid points at his older cousin: 'why hasn't she taken amrit yet? is she doing it wrong?' going by today, what do you say?
o: amrit is your own yes, like the five who stood up in 1699; she'll take it when she's ready.
yes; amrit has a right age, and she's already late for it.
amrit doesn't really matter; it's just an old ceremony.
games.why: in 1699 each of the five stood up on his own, and the Sikh code sets no age. the pace belongs to the person.

practice: If you pray, sit and repeat Waheguru quietly, the simran Sikhs do every day, at whatever pace your breath sets. Don't hurry it and don't drag it.
If you don't pray, sit with one slow sound around you, a fan or your own breathing, and let it keep its own speed.

wordCard.voice: Everyone's pace. No pressure toward amrit, and no judging how fast or slow anyone comes to it.

carryVoice: Your line: amrit waits for your own yes. Five stood up in 1699, each by himself, and Simran's pace belongs to Simran. That's the week.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, section on the amrit ceremony (no age set; willing and old enough to understand), paraphrased
Vaisakhi 1699 at Anandpur: Guru Gobind Singh's call for a head and the five who rose (the Panj Pyare), as told in Sikh tradition, paraphrased
